Andean cloud forests provide a rich backdrop for understanding the life history of the Grass-green tanager (Chlorornis riefferii). Neonates emerge with a modest wet weight at birth of only 6.3 grams [Wwb = 6.3 grams], a value that underscores the altricial condition of the hatchlings. Eggs are incubated at 37 °C [T = 37 °C], and the age at birth or hatching period is 17 days [ab = 17 days], a typical duration for a passerine of this size. Following hatching, the nestling phase is brief but intense, with chicks reaching the fledging stage after just 14 days since birth [tx = 14 days since birth] when maintained under the warm thermal conditions of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C] that characterize the nest microclimate. This rapid nest development is consistent with the high predation pressure often observed in Neotropical montane forests, where a shorter nestling period reduces exposure to risk. The subsequent juvenile phase involves a period of learning to forage independently, laying the groundwork for the slower maturation to come.

Beyond the nest, the trajectory toward adulthood in Chlorornis riefferii unfolds over a longer timescale. The onset of puberty, marking the ability to produce gametes, is reached at 42 days since birth [tp = 42 days since birth] under the typical thermoneutral zone of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]. However, behavioral maturity and territory acquisition often delay first reproduction further. The time since birth at first brood, representing the first successful nesting attempt, is considerably deferred to 1.6 years or approximately 584 days [tR = approximately 584 days] when active at 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]. This lag between physiological puberty and actual breeding is a common pattern among canopy frugivores, likely related to the need to establish a high-quality territory in the competitive Andean forest strata. During this extended sub-adult period, individuals refine their foraging skills on a diet of fruits and some arthropods.

Sexual size dimorphism is evident upon reaching adulthood. The ultimate wet weight attained by mature females stabilizes at 51.6 grams [Wwi = 51.6 grams], while males, which are often more robust in this tanager species, reach a slightly higher typical adult body mass of approximately 54.2 grams [Wwi = approximately 54.2 grams]. This disparity may reflect differential energetic investments, with males possibly requiring greater mass for territorial defense, a behavior that involves vocal displays and active chasing. The body mass values align closely with those of other large-bodied Thraupidae that specialize on a mixed diet of fruit and insects. The energetic demands of maintaining this body mass are significant, and the species exhibits a relatively low daily metabolic throughput for a bird of this size when measured under controlled conditions.

The species' basal metabolic rate provides insight into its energy management strategy. Respirometry trials conducted on resting individuals reveal a maximum basal metabolic rate of 92.73 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = 92.73 milliliters of oxygen per hour] when ambient temperature is at 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]. This rate, measured within the species' thermoneutral zone, is relatively moderate for a passerine of its mass, suggesting an adaptive energy conservation strategy suited to the cool, fluctuating temperatures of high-altitude cloud forests. The elevated thermal conditions required for the BMR measurement, which are warmer than the average forest temperature, imply that the species may have a narrow thermoneutral zone. This physiology supports the species' relatively slow pace of life, contributing to a maximum lifespan that is notably long for a bird of its size.

Integrating these life-history metrics reveals a coherent strategy of delayed reproduction and extended longevity. The maximum lifespan of Chlorornis riefferii is recorded at 11.5 years [am = 11.5 years], a value that represents approximately 4,198 days when active at 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]. This remarkable longevity, coupled with the deferred age at first brood, suggests a life-history that prioritizes adult survival over rapid reproduction. The daily reproductive rate is correspondingly low; females produce a single egg per clutch [N_R_i = single egg per clutch], and typically only one clutch per year [F_R_i = one clutch per year]. This low annual fecundity is typical of long-lived tropical passerines that invest heavily in parental care of the single nestling. The combination of a low reproductive rate, a high adult survival probability, and a long lifespan positions the Grass-green tanager as a classic example of a slow life-history strategy, finely tuned to the stable but resource-limited environment of the Andean cloud forest. This extended lifespan is exceptional among the Thraupidae of comparable body size, where most congeners exhibit maximum lifespans rarely exceeding eight or nine years in the wild.
